conventions.convention: Lebesgue inner measure is the supremum of the measures of compact subsets, with values in [0,+∞].
A Vitali set is a selector for x~y iff x−y∈Q on [0,1], meeting every equivalence class exactly once.
A Bernstein set meets every nonempty perfect subset of R, and its complement does too.
The annulus A(a;r,R) uses strict radial inequalities; neither boundary circle belongs to it, r may be 0, and R may be ∞.
A Laurent series is indexed by all integers and is split into separately locally uniformly convergent nonnegative- and negative-power series.
An isolated singularity is removable if it extends holomorphically, a pole of order m when (z−a)^m f extends holomorphically with nonzero value at a, and essential otherwise.
The residue at an isolated singularity is the Laurent coefficient c_{−1}.
A singularity at infinity is classified through the pulled-back function g(w)=f(1/w) at w=0.
A plane harmonic function is real-valued, C², and satisfies u_xx+u_yy=0.
A harmonic conjugate v of u is defined by holomorphy of u+iv; conjugacy is therefore asymmetric in the named pair.
The circle and disc mean-value properties are required on every positive-radius closed disc contained in the domain; the disc average is normalized by 2/r².
The disc Poisson kernel is P(z,e^{it})=(1−|z|²)/|e^{it}−z|² and its integral uses normalized angular measure dt/(2π).

load_bearing.statement: Let f be holomorphic on A(a;r,R). Then there are complex numbers c_n, n∈Z, such that f(z)=∑_{n∈Z}c_n(z−a)^n for every z in the annulus, and the series converges locally uniformly there.
For a convergent Laurent series on A(a;r,R), c_n=(2πi)^{-1}∫_{|ζ−a|=ρ}f(ζ)/(ζ−a)^{n+1} dζ for every r<ρ<R and n∈Z; consequently the coefficients are unique.
For f holomorphic on 0<|z−a|<R, removability, zero principal part, boundedness near a, existence of a finite limit, and (z−a)f(z)→0 are equivalent.
For f holomorphic on a punctured disc, being a pole, having a finite nonzero principal part, |f(z)|→∞, and holomorphic extendability of 1/f with value 0 are equivalent.
Every plane harmonic function is locally the real part of a holomorphic function.
For 0≤r<1, P_r is positive, has normalized integral 1, and is asserted to converge uniformly to 0 away from the distinguished boundary point as r→1−.
For continuous boundary data, the Poisson integral is harmonic on the disc, extends continuously to the closed disc with the prescribed boundary values, and is unique.
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let V⊆[0,1] be a Vitali set. Then V is not Lebesgue measurable.
Assuming Countable Choice, a Bernstein set B has λ_*(B)=0 and λ^*(B∩I)=λ(I) for every nondegenerate bounded interval I.
Assuming Countable Choice, a measurable A⊆[0,1] invariant under finite changes of binary digits has measure 0 or 1.

concerns.concern: The Statement says that for every x∈[0,1] one should choose “the binary expansion of x that is eventually 0.” Nondyadic reals have no eventually-zero binary expansion, so S_x and hence E_U are undefined for almost every x. The intended convention appears to be the expansion that is not eventually 1, with the terminating expansion chosen at dyadic points.

Claim 3 takes sup over all real θ with |θ|≥δ. Because P_r is 2π-periodic, θ=2π satisfies that inequality but P_r(2π)=P_r(0)=(1+r)/(1−r), which diverges. The claim needs θ represented in [−π,π], or circular distance from 0 at least δ. The proof’s inequality cos θ≤cos δ has the same missing restriction.

Step 1.1 invokes only the local-potential theorem but chooses one holomorphic F on a disc D(a,R) with R>r. Local existence near a does not supply a potential on an arbitrarily prescribed containing disc. The earlier global harmonic-conjugate theorem on homologically simply connected domains would close the route, but it is neither cited nor listed in deps.

For an open or half-open interval I, the set F=I\U in step 1.2 need not be closed in R, so the condensation-point argument cannot be applied as written. A reader can repair the proof by first choosing a closed subinterval J⊂I whose length still exceeds the assumed outer measure and using J\U.

Steps 1.2–3.1 call the two boundary circles a cycle in A(a;ρ,σ), although those circles are excluded by the strict annulus convention. Applying the global Cauchy results in the original annulus A(a;r,R), where the circles lie and the index vanishes off the domain, closes the gap.

Step 2.1 applies the cited Harnack theorem with outer radius R=1 to P(z,1), but that function is singular at the boundary point 1 and is not harmonic on a neighbourhood of the closed unit disc as the cited theorem requires. Applying the theorem first with R<1 and then letting R→1− closes the gap.

Step 1.2 says unboundedness contradicts L3, but L3 is only the forward implication “bounded near the puncture ⇒ extends.” The conclusion is still immediate because any harmonic extension would be continuous and therefore bounded on a smaller closed disc.
